Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(n=250\). The positive divisors of \(250=2\cdot 5^3\) are

\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250.
\]

We will show the minimum is \(499\).

---

## 1. Structure forced by the intersection condition

Taking \(i=j\) gives

\[
|A_i|=i.
\]

If \(i\mid j\), then

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)=i=|A_i|,
\]

so

\[
A_i\subseteq A_j.
\]

Thus for any \(i,j\), if \(g=\gcd(i,j)\), then \(A_g\subseteq A_i\cap A_j\), and since both sets have size \(g\),

\[
A_i\cap A_j=A_g.
\]

For each positive integer \(d\), define

\[
B_d=A_d\setminus \bigcup_{\substack{e\mid d\\ e<d}} A_e.
\]

These sets \(B_d\) are pairwise disjoint: if \(x\in B_d\cap B_e\) with \(d\neq e\), then

\[
x\in A_d\cap A_e=A_{\gcd(d,e)},
\]

where \(\gcd(d,e)<d\), contradicting \(x\in B_d\).

Also, every element of \(A_i\) belongs to exactly one \(B_d\) with \(d\mid i\), so

\[
A_i=\bigsqcup_{d\mid i} B_d.
\]

Therefore

\[
i=|A_i|=\sum_{d\mid i}|B_d|.
\]

By Möbius inversion, or by induction using \(\sum_{d\mid m}\varphi(d)=m\), we get

\[
|B_d|=\varphi(d).
\]

So the whole system is determined by disjoint blocks \(B_d\) of sizes \(\varphi(d)\), with

\[
A_i=\bigcup_{d\mid i} B_d.
\]

---

## 2. Reduction to an ordering problem

We only care about \(d\mid 250\). The relevant elements are

\[
R=\bigcup_{d\mid 250} B_d,
\]

and

\[
|R|=\sum_{d\mid 250}\varphi(d)=250.
\]

List the \(250\) relevant elements in increasing order of their positive integer labels:

\[
r_1<r_2<\cdots<r_{250}.
\]

For each \(d\mid 250\), let \(t_d\) be the largest index such that \(r_{t_d}\in A_d\). Then the maximum element of \(A_d\) is \(r_{t_d}\), so

\[
\max A_d\ge t_d.
\]

Also, if \(e\mid d\), then \(A_e\subseteq A_d\), so

\[
t_e\le t_d.
\]

Order the divisors \(d_1,\dots,d_8\) of \(250\) by nondecreasing \(t_d\), breaking ties so that divisors come before multiples. Then for each \(k\), the set

\[
P_k=\{d_1,\dots,d_k\}
\]

is divisor-closed: if \(x\in P_k\) and \(y\mid x\), then \(y\in P_k\).

Now

\[
\bigcup_{d\in P_k} A_d
=
\bigcup_{e\in P_k} B_e,
\]

so the number of elements in this union is

\[
s_k=\sum_{e\in P_k}\varphi(e).
\]

All of these elements appear among the first \(t_{d_k}\) relevant elements, hence

\[
t_{d_k}\ge s_k.
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d
\ge
\sum_{k=1}^8 t_{d_k}
\ge
\sum_{k=1}^8 s_k.
\]

But \(s_k=\sum_{j=1}^k \varphi(d_j)\) is exactly the completion time of the \(k\)-th job in a linear extension of the divisibility poset, where the job corresponding to \(d\) has processing time \(\varphi(d)\). Thus we need to minimize

\[
\sum_{k=1}^8 \sum_{j=1}^k \varphi(d_j)
\]

over all linear extensions of the divisors of \(250\).

The relevant processing times are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1 & 2 & 5 & 10 & 25 & 50 & 125 & 250\\
\hline
\varphi(d) & 1 & 1 & 4 & 4 & 20 & 20 & 100 & 100
\end{array}
\]

with the rule that a divisor must appear before any of its multiples.

---

## 3. Optimal ordering of the eight jobs

Clearly \(1\) is first and \(250\) is last. We now determine the rest.

### \(2\) must precede \(5\)

Suppose \(5\) appears before \(2\). The only jobs that can appear between \(5\) and \(2\) are \(25\) and possibly \(125\). Moving \(2\) to the position immediately after \(1\) keeps the order valid and leaves all later completion times unchanged. The affected segment improves in every possible case:

\[
\begin{aligned}
5,2 &: 4+5=9 \quad\leadsto\quad 2,5: 1+5=6,\\
5,25,2 &: 4+24+25=53 \quad\leadsto\quad 2,5,25: 1+5+25=31,\\
5,25,125,2 &: 4+24+124+125=277 \quad\leadsto\quad 2,5,25,125: 1+5+25+125=156.
\end{aligned}
\]

So \(2\) precedes \(5\). Then after \(1,2\), the only available job is \(5\), so the order begins

\[
1,2,5.
\]

### \(10\) must precede \(25\)

Now suppose \(25\) appears before \(10\). The only possible intervening job is \(125\). Moving \(10\) to just after \(1,2,5\) improves the sum:

\[
\begin{aligned}
25,10 &: 20+24=44 \quad\leadsto\quad 10,25: 4+24=28,\\
25,125,10 &: 20+120+124=264 \quad\leadsto\quad 10,25,125: 4+24+124=152.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(10\) precedes \(25\), and then \(25\) is forced next. So far we have

\[
1,2,5,10,25.
\]

### \(50\) must precede \(125\)

After \(1,2,5,10,25\), the available jobs are \(50\) and \(125\). If \(125\) were before \(50\), swapping them changes

\[
100+120=220
\]

to

\[
20+120=140,
\]

an improvement. Hence \(50\) precedes \(125\), and then \(250\) is last.

Thus the optimal order is

\[
1,\;2,\;5,\;10,\;25,\;50,\;125,\;250.
\]

The corresponding prefix sums are

\[
1,\;2,\;6,\;10,\;30,\;50,\;150,\;250.
\]

Their sum is

\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

So every valid sequence satisfies

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d\ge 499.
\]

---

## 4. Construction attaining \(499\)

Define disjoint blocks for the divisors of \(250\) as follows:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B_1&=\{1\},\\
B_2&=\{2\},\\
B_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
B_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
B_{25}&=\{11,12,\dots,30\},\\
B_{50}&=\{31,32,\dots,50\},\\
B_{125}&=\{51,52,\dots,150\},\\
B_{250}&=\{151,152,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For every other positive integer \(d\), choose \(B_d\) to be any set of \(\varphi(d)\) unused positive integers, all larger than \(250\). Then define

\[
A_m=\bigcup_{d\mid m}B_d.
\]

For any \(i,j\),

\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigcup_{d\mid i,\ d\mid j}B_d
=
\bigcup_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)}B_d,
\]

so

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|
=
\sum_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)}\varphi(d)
=
\gcd(i,j).
\]

Thus this construction is valid.

The required maxima are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1 & 2 & 5 & 10 & 25 & 50 & 125 & 250\\
\hline
\max A_d & 1 & 2 & 6 & 10 & 30 & 50 & 150 & 250
\end{array}
\]

and their sum is again

\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

Therefore the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
